query: What diagnostics and test statistics reliably detect non-normal random effects, heteroscedastic residuals, informative cluster-size, and cluster-level attrition in multilevel models?

response.query: What diagnostics and test statistics reliably detect non-normal random effects, heteroscedastic residuals, informative cluster-size, and cluster-level attrition in multilevel models?
response.answer: To detect non-normal random effects, use diagnostic plots like Q-Q plots; for heteroscedasticity, apply Levene's test; for cluster-level attrition, check dropout patterns; and for cluster size effects, use intraclass correlation coefficients.

results.title: Reference effect measures for quantifying, comparing and visualizing variation from random and fixed effects in non-normal multilevel models, with applications to site variation in medical procedure use and outcomes | BMC Medical Research Methodology
results.content: # Reference effect measures for quantifying, comparing and visualizing variation from random and fixed effects in non-normal multilevel models, with applications to site variation in medical procedure use and outcomes. Reference effect measures for quantifying, comparing and visualizing variation from random and fixed effects in non-normal multilevel models, with applications to site variation in medical procedure use and outcomes. We propose a Reference Effect Measure (REM) approach to 1) quantify GCE and compare it to individual subject and cluster covariate effects, and 2) quantify relative magnitudes of GCE and variation from sets of measured factors. In this paper we consider two objectives in the analysis of cluster variation for non-normal outcomes in multilevel designs: 1) Quantify GCE and compare it to individual subject and cluster covariate effects, and 2) Quantify relative magnitudes of GCE and variation from sets of measured factors. We can also use REM to compare the effect of a 1 unit increase in a covariate *x**k* to unmeasured cluster variation by calculating \( \upphi \left(\frac{\beta\_k}{\sigma\_u}\right) \), which provides the equivalent percentile in the random effects distribution. Variation explained by a set of covariates *x**s* can be quantified by calculating the empirical distribution of odds ratios for each subject compared with a subject of median risk within the empirical distribution of {***x***'***sij******β******s***}, all in a cluster with the same unmeasured characteristics *u* and holding constant all other measured characteristics, designated by ***x***−***s***. Benefits of the REM approach include expression on the odds ratio scale, and accommodation of non-normal random effect or empirical distributions through use of percentiles, all of which facilitate numerical and graphical comparisons between all sets of fixed and random factors considered. We describe and illustrate several ways of presenting REM results including *REM*(0.75) for moderate comparisons, *REM*(0.975) for extreme comparisons, and 95% ranges that enclose 95% of the distribution of odds ratios compared with the median to describe the variation in risk of mortality patients may face based on opposite extremes in the distribution of GCE or a set of factors. *et al.* Reference effect measures for quantifying, comparing and visualizing variation from random and fixed effects in non-normal multilevel models, with applications to site variation in medical procedure use and outcomes.

results.content: Home » mlmhelper: An R helper package for estimating multilevel models. # mlmhelper: An R helper package for estimating multilevel models. # mlmhelper: An R helper package for estimating multilevel models. # mlmhelper: An R helper package for estimating multilevel models. mlmhelpr is a collection of helper functions designed to streamline the process of running multilevel or linear mixed models in R. The package assists users with common tasks such as computing the intraclass correlation and design effect, centering variables, and estimating the proportion of variance explained at each level. Additionally, students often expressed frustration that lme4, the primary R package for estimating multilevel models, did not provide all the necessary information required by our textbooks and readings. mlmhelpr offers tests and statistics from many popular multilevel modeling textbooks such as Raudenbush and Bryk (2002), Hox et al. This function refits a model using grand-mean centering, group-mean/within cluster centering (if a grouping variable is specified), or centering at a user-specified value. This function performs a Hausman test to test for differences between random- and fixed-effects models. This test determines whether there are significant differences between fixed-effect and random-effect models with similar specifications. If the test statistic is not statistically significant, a random effects model (i.e. a multilevel model) may be more suitable (i.e., efficient). No unique intra-class correlation can be calculated when a random slope is present in the model.” However, Snijders and Bosker (2012) offer a calculation to derive this value (equation 7.9), and their approach is implemented. Levene’s test computes a one-way analysis of variance of the level-2 grouping variable on the squared residuals of the model. A likelihood ratio test is used to compare this model with a null model that regresses the squared residuals on an empty model with the same random effects. This function computes the proportion of variance explained for each random effect level in the model (i.e., level-1, level-2) as discussed by Raudenbush & Bryk (2002, p. This function computes reliability coefficients for random effects according to Raudenbush and Bryk (2002) and Snijders and Bosker (2012). This function computes robust standard errors for linear models. If you use R to estimate multilevel models, give mlmhelpr a try, and let me know if you find any errors or mistakes.

Journal of Statistical Computation and Simulation Volume 88, 2018 - Issue 16 The effect of number of clusters and cluster size on statistical power and Type I error rates when testing random effects variance components in multilevel linear and logistic regression models AustinInstitute for Clinical Evaluative Sciences, Toronto, ON, Canada;Institute of Health Management, Policy and Evaluation, University of Toronto, Toronto, ON, Canada;Schulich Heart Research Program, Sunnybrook Research Institute, Toronto, ON, Canada Correspondencepeter.austin@ George LeckieCentre for Multilevel Modelling, University of Bristol, Bristol, UKView further author information Pages 3151-3163 | Received 23 Jan 2018, Accepted 22 Jul 2018, Published online: 07 Aug 2018 In this article Article contents Related research Notation and statistical tests for null variance Monte Carlo simulations of power and type I error rates * View PDF (open in a new window)PDF (open in a new window) Formulae display:- [x] : MathJax Logo? When using multilevel regression models that incorporate cluster-specific random effects, the Wald and the likelihood ratio (LR) tests are used for testing the null hypothesis that the variance of the random effects distribution is equal to zero. We conducted a series of Monte Carlo simulations to examine the effect of the number of clusters and the number of subjects per cluster on the statistical power to detect a non-null random effects variance and to compare the empirical type I error rates of the Wald and LR tests. Similarly, this may explain why, for a given value of the VPC, number of clusters and number of subjects per cluster, statistical power was greater when using the likelihood ratio test with the linear model compared to with the logistic model.
